name: Hyaluronic acid filler
lead: Hyaluronic acid (HA) fillers are injectable gels, most often based on cross-linked hyaluronic acid, placed under the skin to restore volume, soften folds and wrinkles, and reshape areas such as the lips, cheeks, chin and the nasolabial folds beside the mouth. Hyaluronic acid is a naturally occurring component of skin, and reviews describe HA gels as the most commonly used dermal filler.[2] Well-known product lines include Juvederm and Restylane, and a large range of other brands, including Korean and European products, is discussed in appearance communities.[19][20][26]

For looks, the practical appeal is that a few millilitres of gel can change facial proportions in a single short visit without surgery: fuller or more defined lips, projected cheeks and chin, a smoother line from the nose to the mouth, and a less hollow midface or under-eye area. Clinicians describe HA fillers as temporary and reversible, because the gel can be dissolved with the enzyme hyaluronidase, and the visible effect may outlast the physical gel because of possible collagen stimulation.[2][3][23]

Randomized trials and systematic reviews report that most side effects are short-lived injection-site reactions such as swelling, tenderness and bruising, while rare complications, including vascular occlusion and vision loss, can be serious and in some cases permanent.[4][1][10][21] The US Food and Drug Administration regulates fillers as medical devices and advises that they be injected only by trained providers.[21] In looksmaxxing discussions the procedure appears mainly as a non-surgical option for lips, cheeks, chin and under-eye hollows, usually discussed alongside implants, fat grafting and surgery, and with attention to which product suits which facial area.[25][26][27] Evidence for volume and wrinkle correction is extensive, while the published evidence on facial attractiveness specifically is limited to a small number of studies.[5][8]

paras: HA fillers are sterile gels of hyaluronic acid, a sugar-based polymer found in skin and connective tissue that binds water.[2][13] Chemically it is a non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan made of repeating units of glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine, and its negatively charged groups let it hold large amounts of water.[18] Products differ in how heavily the HA is cross-linked, in particle size and in stiffness, and these physical properties influence how a gel behaves in different facial areas.[13] Most commercial HA fillers use a chemical cross-linker, commonly BDDE, to resist breakdown by enzymes in tissue; a 2024 review has raised questions about the long-term safety of BDDE.[15]

Native, uncross-linked HA is broken down within about half a day, which is why cross-linking is used to make a filler last months rather than hours.[20] Reviews describe the gel as working by filling and volumizing, and also by attracting water to the injected area.[2] Some research has reported that cross-linked HA injected into photodamaged skin was followed by new collagen production, which may partly explain why effects can outlast the gel itself.[7][2]

Karl Meyer and John Palmer first isolated hyaluronic acid from the vitreous of a cow's eye in 1934.[18] Its first major biomedical product was Healon, developed by Pharmacia in the 1970s and 1980s as a viscous lubricant for eye surgery, and manufacturers later used cross-linking and stabilisation methods to extend its short half-life in tissue.[18]

Before HA, injectables for the face had a mixed history. Surgeons tried injecting paraffin into the lips around 1900 without success, liquid silicone was used from the early 1960s but abandoned about thirty years later over health and appearance concerns, and injectable bovine collagen became the standard by about 1980, though it required an allergy test and a wait before treatment.[22] The late 1990s and 2000s brought more materials, including calcium hydroxylapatite, PMMA microsphere fillers and fat transfer, alongside the first HA products.[22]

HA was first approved for facial tissue augmentation in Europe in 1996, and the US FDA approved Juvederm in June 2006; in a pre-approval study of 146 subjects over 24 weeks, Juvederm gave more persistent correction than a bovine collagen filler and 88% of subjects preferred the Juvederm-treated fold.[20] Restylane is described as the first HA filler approved by the FDA for cosmetic injection into facial subdermal tissue, and is made by Galderma.[19] Hyaluronidase products used to dissolve filler also entered US medicine in this period: Vitrase and Amphadase were approved in 2004, Hydase in 2005 and the recombinant human product Hylenex in December 2005.[23]

The American Society of Plastic Surgeons data cited on one encyclopedia page counted 778,000 Restylane injections in 2006.[22] Dermal fillers are described in the research literature as among the most popular cosmetic procedures.[1] A Dutch physician's 2007 description of a 'fern pattern' injection technique is one example of how injection methods continued to be published and refined.[19]

Reported uses include correcting nasolabial folds, augmenting the lips, restoring midface volume and softening fine perioral lines.[1][5] Lip enhancement for volume and contour is described as the most common use of Restylane, with other indications including aging lines, hollows around the eyes and cheek and chin contouring.[19] Juvederm is described as used for deep folds, lip plumping and filling hollow areas and facial scars.[20]

The FDA lists approved uses of absorbable fillers as moderate to severe facial wrinkles and folds, lip augmentation and augmentation of the cheeks, chin and back of the hand, in adults aged 22 and over. Uses it lists as not approved include injection into the glabella, nose, periorbital area, forehead and neck, and body contouring such as breast or buttock augmentation.[21] Clinicians do sometimes treat areas outside the labeled indications, and the under-eye hollow is a frequent subject of questions from users in appearance forums.[28]

A related use is the so-called skin booster, in which low-concentration HA products are placed in the dermis for hydration rather than volume; one review of the concept has since been retracted by its journal.[14] Clinicians also use HA to alter facial contour, for example in cheek augmentation, which one clinical trial linked to improved self-rated feelings of facial attractiveness.[8]

Lips are the best-documented use. A meta-analysis of lip augmentation covering 32 records in its descriptive review and 10 in its quantitative synthesis reported that the share of subjects with at least a one-point gain in lip fullness was 91% at two months, 74% at six months and 46% at twelve months.[5] Cheeks and the midface are treated to restore volume and projection, and the chin is a growing area of interest; looksmax.org users describe jawline and chin fillers such as Juvederm Volux, with one reporting results similar to Voluma on the chin but more discomfort and soreness for two weeks afterward.[25]

Overfilled lips are sometimes described in media and online as a 'trout pout', a term that an encyclopedia entry on lip augmentation notes is used mockingly, and it says that surgeon skill is described as critical to outcomes.[22]

Reviews describe HA gels as varying in cross-linking, particle size and stiffness, and these properties, studied under the heading of rheology, influence how a gel lifts tissue and how it moves with the face.[2][13] A long looksmax.org guide on choosing a filler summarises rheology metrics such as G-prime (stiffness) and cohesivity and lists Korean filler brands by facial area, while carrying a disclaimer that it is educational and that self-injection carries extreme risks including vascular occlusion and blindness.[26] Clinicians, on the other hand, base product and depth choices on the area treated, the tissue present and their own technique, and the same guide notes that individual anatomy and the injector's technique determine results.[26][4]

The lip meta-analysis concluded that HA is an effective lip filler, with responder rates declining over twelve months, and called for more well-designed randomized trials.[5] A split-face comparison of fillers has examined collagen and elastin stimulation after HA injection versus calcium hydroxylapatite,[6] and a controlled trial reported collagen production in photodamaged skin after cross-linked HA injection.[7]

Trials also compare HA with other products or combinations, such as a randomized study of botulinum toxin combined with a skin-booster HA product for periorbital wrinkles[16] and a registered comparison of two HA fillers' non-inferiority in wrinkle correction.[29] Duration varies by product, site and individual; general overviews describe effects commonly lasting about six months to longer, with repeat treatment needed to maintain results, and note that physical activity can shorten the lifespan of a filler.[15]

On attractiveness specifically, a 2012 trial enrolled ten women aged 40 to 60 who received cheek augmentation with an HA filler; seven of ten rated their own appearance 0.5 to 2 points better on a six-point scale after two weeks, and the author concluded that cheek augmentation improves how women feel about their attractiveness.[8]

Controlled human research includes a meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials on adverse events by facial location,[1] a systematic review of 48 high-level randomized studies on safety,[4] a meta-analysis of lip augmentation,[5] a randomized split-face histology study comparing HA with calcium hydroxylapatite,[6] a controlled trial of collagen production in photodamaged skin,[7] and the small trial of cheek augmentation and self-rated attractiveness.[8] ClinicalTrials.gov also lists registered studies of HA fillers for midface volume, lip appearance in specific populations and comparisons between HA products.[29][30]

A systematic review of 48 high-level-evidence randomized studies grouped adverse events into expected reactions, product- or technique-related events and severe events, and found that most were short-lived injection-site reactions that resolved on their own within weeks; severe events were rare, lasted months and needed active care.[4] A meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials found significant differences at the nasolabial fold compared with other sites for swelling, lumps and firmness, but no significant difference for pain, redness, bruising, tenderness, itching or discoloration.[1] In the lip meta-analysis of 1,496 participants, the most frequent treatment-related events were tenderness (88.8%), swelling (74.3%) and bruising (39.5%), with foreign-body granulomas in 0.6%.[5] The FDA lists bruising, redness, swelling, pain, itching and rash as common, with nodules, infection and tissue death less common.[21]

The FDA identifies accidental injection into a blood vessel as the most serious risk, which can block blood flow and cause tissue death, vision problems including blindness, and stroke, some of them permanent.[21] Review authors describe vision loss as often irreversible.[10][9][12] A 2019 update reviewed 48 new cases of vision loss reported between January 2015 and September 2018; HA caused 81.3% of them, the nose was the highest-risk region (56.3%), followed by the glabella (27.1%), forehead (18.8%) and nasolabial fold (14.6%), and 20.8% of patients fully recovered vision and 16.7% partly recovered, with no treatment shown to be consistently successful.[10] A general reference notes that embolic complications are more frequent with autologous fat, followed by HA.[15]

Delayed nodules, infection and hypersensitivity reactions have also been described, and the FDA notes that some effects can appear weeks, months or years after injection.[12][3][21] Published guidance recommends prompt recognition and treatment of occlusion, including high-dose hyaluronidase protocols, although controlled data are limited and recommendations differ between expert groups.[9][11][3][17] A 2021 guideline describes defined stages of ischemia that show the extent and timing of tissue damage.[9]

The FDA advises delaying treatment when the skin is inflamed or infected or when a bleeding disorder is present, and says safety has not been established in pregnancy, breastfeeding, people under 22, people prone to keloids, repeated long-term use or use together with neuromodulators.[21] Listed contraindications for Restylane include severe allergies, active infection at the site, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and bleeding disorders or blood-thinner use.[19] Allergy testing is advised for certain materials, particularly animal-derived ones.[21]

HA fillers are not pharmacologically active in the usual sense. Reviews describe them as biodegradable, with a negligible risk of immune or allergic reaction compared with some other fillers, and rapidly degraded by hyaluronidase.[2][13] Hyaluronidase is a family of enzymes that break down HA; the injectable form is prescription-only in the US, the UK and Australia, and one reference describes it as the best treatment option for dissolving lip filler or addressing related complications.[23][3] The FDA notes that removing filler can be difficult or impossible, particularly for permanent products, which is a different situation from HA.[21]

In the United States dermal fillers are regulated as medical devices; the FDA states that no fillers are approved for over-the-counter use, that injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic use, and that people should not inject themselves or buy fillers online because counterfeit or unapproved products may be sold.[21] In the UK and European Economic Area they require a CE mark, which certifies manufacturing standards rather than clinical efficacy, and more than 140 such products are cited.[15] In England it has been a criminal offence since 1 October 2021 to administer cosmetic fillers or botulinum toxin to anyone under 18, under an Act that received Royal Assent on 29 April 2021.[24] Who qualifies to inject fillers, doctors or licensed non-physician injectors, is debated.[15]

On looksmax.org filler appears as a reversible, non-surgical route to proportions, discussed alongside implants and surgery. Threads include questions about jawline and chin fillers such as Volux and Voluma,[25] an in-depth guide on rheology and brand choice,[26] a long personal account of an 'ascension' that features Juvederm,[27] and users asking about experiences with Restylane under the eyes.[28] Posters say reversibility with hyaluronidase makes fillers a lower-commitment option than implants, while others stress, as the rheology guide does, that professional injection is required.[26]

The FDA warns against buying fillers online, noting that counterfeit or unapproved products may be sold.[21] Looksmax.org's own filler guide carries a disclaimer that self-injection carries extreme risks, including blindness, tissue death and permanent scarring.[26] Public debate also covers how natural or overfilled results look, the minimum age for treatment, and the training of injectors.[22][24][15]

Other fillers and volume methods include calcium hydroxylapatite, poly-L-lactic acid, PMMA microsphere fillers, autologous fat transfer and surgical implants.[15][22] Several studies have identified fat grafting as one of the better methods for a semi-permanent fuller lip, though it involves a donor site and can cause lumping or scarring.[22] Botulinum toxin is often combined with filler for upper-face wrinkles, although the FDA says safety of combined use with neuromodulators has not been established.[16][21] Natural HA is also injected into joints for osteoarthritis and used in eye surgery and wound care, which are separate from cosmetic filler use.[18]

lore.intro: HA filler is discussed in appearance communities as the standard reversible, non-surgical injectable, often compared with implants, fat grafting and surgery for lips, cheeks and chin, and with attention to products, rheology and injector choice.[25][26][27]

claims.claim: HA filler is a safe, reversible way to change facial proportions
claims.believers: Proponents point to the fact that the gel can be dissolved with hyaluronidase if the result is unwanted, which they see as making filler lower-risk than implants.[26]
claims.experts: Reviews describe HA fillers as reversible with hyaluronidase and most adverse events as short-lived, but report that vascular occlusion and blindness, though rare, can be permanent.[2][4][10] The FDA states that the most serious risk is accidental injection into a blood vessel.[21]

claims.claim: Cheek and midface filler makes the face look more attractive
claims.believers: Users describe volume in the cheeks and chin as an easy way to improve contour and perceived youthfulness.[27][25]
claims.experts: A small clinical trial reported improved self-rated feelings of attractiveness after cheek augmentation; research on observer-rated attractiveness is limited.[8]

claims.claim: HA filler stimulates the skin's own collagen
claims.believers: Some practitioners and users say filler leaves lasting skin quality improvements beyond the gel.
claims.experts: Biopsy-based studies have reported collagen production after cross-linked HA injection, and reviews note the effect may outlast the gel.[7][2]

claims.claim: Chin and jawline filler can substitute for implants or surgery
claims.believers: Looksmax.org users compare jawline and chin fillers such as Volux and Voluma and ask about chin projection from them, treating filler as a non-surgical option.[25]
claims.experts: Reviews and the FDA label describe filler as temporary, with effects often lasting about six months to a year or more.[15][22] The FDA lists chin augmentation among approved uses of absorbable fillers.[21]

claims.claim: Choosing a filler by its rheology (stiffness and cohesivity) matches the product to the area
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide summarises rheology metrics and recommends brands by facial area, presenting them as benchmarks for choosing a product.[26]
claims.experts: Reviews confirm that cross-linking, particle size and stiffness influence how HA gels behave in different areas;[2][13] the guide itself notes that anatomy, metabolism and injector technique determine results.[26]

claims.claim: Under-eye filler is a standard fix for hollows
claims.believers: Users ask about others' experiences with Restylane under the eyes as a treatment for hollows.[28]
claims.experts: The FDA lists injection into the periorbital area among uses that are not approved, and the vision-loss review identifies the nose, glabella, forehead and nasolabial fold as the highest-risk regions in reported cases.[21][10]

claims.claim: Filler results can be dissolved at any time, so mistakes are easy to undo
claims.believers: Posters value the availability of hyaluronidase as an undo option.[26]
claims.experts: Hyaluronidase is prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia and is described as an effective way to dissolve HA filler,[23] but guidelines note that controlled data on dosing for emergencies are limited and expert recommendations differ.[9][11][3]

claims.claim: Fillers can be self-injected or bought online
claims.believers: Discussion of cheaper or gray-market products appears in appearance communities, though the major looksmax.org guide itself warns against self-injection.[26]
claims.experts: The FDA states that people should not inject themselves or buy fillers online because products may be counterfeit or unapproved, and that no fillers are approved for over-the-counter use.[21]

card.summary: The standard injectable filler: reversible gel for lips, cheeks and folds, well studied for volume, rare but serious vascular risks.
card.note: Rare vascular occlusion can cause tissue loss or permanent vision loss; provider skill matters.

quick.overview:
Hyaluronic acid fillers are injectable gels used to add volume and smooth folds in the lips, cheeks and lines around the mouth. They are the most widely used type of dermal filler, and randomized trials and meta-analyses support their effect on volume and wrinkles.

Results are temporary, commonly lasting around six months or longer depending on product and area, and the gel can be dissolved with an enzyme if the result is unwanted.
quick.mechanism: The gel physically fills space and binds water, and some studies report that it also prompts nearby skin cells to make new collagen.
quick.risks: Most side effects are short-lived swelling, redness and bruising. Rare but serious complications include blocked blood vessels causing tissue death and, in the worst cases, permanent vision loss; guidelines describe emergency treatment with hyaluronidase. In the US fillers are regulated as medical devices and injected by licensed providers.
